evidence.quote: So you're the Global Head of Product at Square. Square is part of a holding company, and maybe we can start there. Can you explain a little bit more about how the companies, or the teams, are designed?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, definitely. I've been at Square, slash Block, for many years. I've seen really every evolution of the company, from the little white reader all the way through to the sophisticated multiple ecosystems we have. It's unique to be at a company that has not only been able to innovate on one product, but then create multiple ecosystems of products throughout its journey. Maybe I'll start with how my journey here began. My company was acquired, I was CTO, and I grew up through the engineering org here. We had a general-management model for many years, so this was business-unit focused. And then about two years ago, we reordered the entire company to be more focused on our customers, functionalizing everything. One of the key reasons we did that was we believed functional excellence, i.e. excellence within your domain, engineering, product, design, and so on, was really important, and that some of the other org models we'd had previously reduced the craft and excellence we wanted to see within each of our functions. So the past two or so years, we've been in a fully functional world where there are top-line orgs: product, design, engineering. And within that we have brand-based focus areas, Square, Cash App, and so on. From an org-design perspective, there are many ways we could take the conversation, but one of the key things is you want to focus orgs around customer outcomes as much as possible. The farther you go from that principle, the worse outcomes you get. Why Square Killed the Business-Unit Model
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: Great. So it's the Square brand, and I lead product for the Square brand. The way we've decided to organize the Square org is leaning into a couple of beliefs I have for building products. One is you want teams as close to customer outcomes as possible, so they can really understand the needs of the customers and build products to serve those needs. That's led us to a couple of broad orgs. First is an audiences org: these are all of our verticals, think services, retail, food and beverage, and so on. Then a core platform org. But the core platform org importantly also has product services it's responsible for. I think it's very easy for platform teams to fall into a kind of "one size fits none" when they're building software, thinking about a very generic solution that doesn't solve any needs. So it's important to marry product and platform together in certain areas. Then we have a growth team, so the whole acquisition flywheel. And a money team, so money for us is everything from bill pay, payroll, banking, and so on. And then obviously we have our hardware teams, which is a sister org to us. Integrating Hardware and Software
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: Yeah, the real world is definitely not on X every day, though some are. Small business is fascinating, because they're the most pure instantiation of an entrepreneur. They literally put their livelihood on the line for their passion, and that passion could be anything from candlestick making to bakeries to really anything. I find that endlessly fascinating, and I respect it a lot. Small business, in my opinion, really forms the artery, or the core, of the economy. The main streets of the world are unique. They're really important social areas for different economies and neighborhoods. What Square and Block have always stood for is economic empowerment, and what that means for Square is making sure neighborhoods can thrive. We say we want Main Street to stand as tall as Wall Street. That's really important, because to do so, they need technology. You can't compete today in the business landscape without automating parts of your business with software, and now increasingly with artificial intelligence. I firmly believe that if you take advanced technology and democratize it, give it to as many people, as many small businesses, as possible, that's net good for the economy and net good for society. So those are some of the things I spend a lot of time on. And it's not easy, because each of these businesses is endlessly unique. They need very specific workflows. A bakery is just different from a flower shop, and that's different from a burger joint. They have different people, different teams, different workflows. So it's all different, and that's one of the awesome things we've been able to do at Square. Bringing AI to People Who Aren't Tech Savvy
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: So I'm thinking about your overall TAM, because in a way, Square started as a payments company, and now it seems like it's an entire ecosystem. How are you thinking about that, and the larger TAM?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, I actually have a hot take on TAM. My hot take is that with the right team, the right idea, and the right learning loop, your TAM is almost infinite. What I mean is that you can create markets with incredible products. That's important for Square, in that we have effectively endless TAM, because it's the small, medium, even enterprise economy, which is trillions of dollars. The two important things for building products and software in these very large TAM markets are, one, you need some forcing function to help teams and people make decisions. We at Square believe in local economies and neighborhoods, and our North Star is to build what we call a neighborhood network, which is effectively all the economic action that happens in a neighborhood: small business owners, their staff, and the customers coming into those businesses. The interesting thing about focusing on local neighborhoods is that it refocuses the TAM away from things like internet-only, direct-to-consumer websites; that's not part of a local economy. What you can start to do is look at Main Street, look at your local neighborhoods, and see what kinds of businesses exist there. So you have an ideal customer: these are the sets of customers I want to build for. And then you can help teams make decisions: "Great, we're going to solve those needs, across commerce tools, both online and offline; financial tools, banking, checking, credit; and then intelligence tools." Because intelligence and autonomy is a core part of building software and helping local neighborhoods be better. Consolidating the SMB's Fragmented Tools
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

You have a vision of what you want to build, but the path there takes a bunch of different turns as you figure out what defect rates you're targeting, what reliability rates, battery life, and so on. evidence.quote: Yeah, it's a good question. Running a business is difficult, and not for the most obvious reason. Yes, obviously you have to hire and do your craft, whether that's food or whatever. But it's also a kind of loneliness, where you don't always know where to go or what decisions to make. For example, what should you price a menu item at? What should you price your burger? Sure, you could calculate how much it costs you to make the burger, but should you mark it up by 10% or 20%? There's an endless set of decisions. Sometimes you hear small business owners start working the second there's another head still on the pillow in their bed, and they keep working all the way through the evening, because there's always some decision they have to make. The advantage, or the attraction, of AI for business is not just a chatbot; it's really to have this intelligent thought partner that lets businesses make better decisions, and then eventually offload and delegate full tasks to parts of their business. A couple of examples could be inventory intake, or spotting sales trends for your business and then suggesting a marketing campaign, or a number of other unique workflows. The interesting part is that the days of just a standard question-answer chatbot are kind of over, for a few reasons. First, we've basically already solved that problem, and what people are expecting now is to do real work with AI. Real work is far more than answering questions and getting some answers back in a thread. Real work looks like synthesizing data across all of your data sources. It looks like creating artifacts specifically for your business. That could be something like an inventory workflow for the bakery we're talking about, or a sales leaderboard so you can train and incentivize your staff. entities.how_described: 本集说 Willem 对 TAM 的激进观点是：有了对的团队、对的想法、对的学习循环，TAM 几乎是无限的，好产品能创造市场

evidence.quote: Square started as a payments company, and now it seems like it's an entire ecosystem. How are you thinking about the larger TAM?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Well, I actually have a hot take on TAM. My hot take on TAM is that... Introduction
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Willem Avé, Global Head of Product at Square. He landed there in 2014 when Square acquired BookFresh, the scheduling startup he co-founded and ran as CTO. So he has watched this thing go from a little white card reader to multiple ecosystems inside Block. And his customers are not on X all day; they run bakeries. Here's what we'll cover: why they tore up the business-unit model and went fully functional. The DRI model built to kill the silent veto. What happens when AI encodes the knowledge your org chart used to hold. The chatbot era is over, and what replaces it. And his hot take that TAM is almost infinite. Let's get into it.
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, that's exactly right. A few things are true. One, I love what you said: you don't want sellers or customers to do more work. That's a very important insight. My experience, and a lot of people's experience using AI, is that you just get a bunch of word vomit, effectively. You get a bunch of data and you have to parse it, and that's actually work. Sometimes it's very useful, if you're doing research or whatnot. But other times it's like, "Please shorten that for me," or "Just create me a little website or something." The more you can steer these experiences to very high value, without causing customers to do a lot of work to use it, the more that builds trust with the system, and then it allows you to delegate and take actions. I didn't show this in the demo, but you can do bulk actions, you can create campaigns, all of that great stuff within the same experience. One of the interesting things, at least for small business, is that a lot of the time people don't just wake up and go, "Oh, I have to change the price of X." Usually you have to do some investigation. So you get some questions and detailed analyses, and then you have enough trust in the system to say, "Okay, now I'll go delegate some work to it to actually execute on inventory counts or price changes." A Hot Take on TAM: Almost Infinite
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: So I'm thinking about your overall TAM, because in a way, Square started as a payments company, and now it seems like it's an entire ecosystem. How are you thinking about that, and the larger TAM?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah, I actually have a hot take on TAM. My hot take is that with the right team, the right idea, and the right learning loop, your TAM is almost infinite. What I mean is that you can create markets with incredible products. That's important for Square, in that we have effectively endless TAM, because it's the small, medium, even enterprise economy, which is trillions of dollars. The two important things for building products and software in these very large TAM markets are, one, you need some forcing function to help teams and people make decisions. We at Square believe in local economies and neighborhoods, and our North Star is to build what we call a neighborhood network, which is effectively all the economic action that happens in a neighborhood: small business owners, their staff, and the customers coming into those businesses. The interesting thing about focusing on local neighborhoods is that it refocuses the TAM away from things like internet-only, direct-to-consumer websites; that's not part of a local economy. What you can start to do is look at Main Street, look at your local neighborhoods, and see what kinds of businesses exist there. So you have an ideal customer: these are the sets of customers I want to build for. And then you can help teams make decisions: "Great, we're going to solve those needs, across commerce tools, both online and offline; financial tools, banking, checking, credit; and then intelligence tools." Because intelligence and autonomy is a core part of building software and helping local neighborhoods be better. Consolidating the SMB's Fragmented Tools
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

entities.name: 硬件 (hardware)
entities.how_described: 本集说硬件出现在商家的真实物理空间里，必须平易近人、易用、令人愉悦，关键是要将软件形态与硬件形态结合，不能分开想

evidence.quote: One of the unique things about your product is that you have a hardware component as well as software. So I'm curious to know how you integrate those two worlds as part of the same function.
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Hardware must be approachable. It must be easy to use. It must be completely delightful, and doing so is not easy.
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: Great. So it's the Square brand, and I lead product for the Square brand. The way we've decided to organize the Square org is leaning into a couple of beliefs I have for building products. One is you want teams as close to customer outcomes as possible, so they can really understand the needs of the customers and build products to serve those needs. That's led us to a couple of broad orgs. First is an audiences org: these are all of our verticals, think services, retail, food and beverage, and so on. Then a core platform org. But the core platform org importantly also has product services it's responsible for. I think it's very easy for platform teams to fall into a kind of "one size fits none" when they're building software, thinking about a very generic solution that doesn't solve any needs. So it's important to marry product and platform together in certain areas. Then we have a growth team, so the whole acquisition flywheel. And a money team, so money for us is everything from bill pay, payroll, banking, and so on. And then obviously we have our hardware teams, which is a sister org to us. Integrating Hardware and Software
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: I was literally going to ask about that, because one of the unique things about your product is that you have a hardware component as well as software. So I'm curious to know how you integrate those two worlds as part of the same function.
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: Yeah. Hardware is something very special, and we have one of the best hardware teams on the planet. What I mean by special is that hardware shows up in businesses' real worlds. It's something you put on the counter, something you carry with you during your shift, something you use. So hardware must be approachable. It must be easy to use. It must be completely delightful. And doing so is not easy. The magic really happens when you integrate hardware and software together in a way that builds delightful experiences. Almost everyone's used an iPhone; they set the bar for a lot of that software-hardware integration. The key is making sure that when you're building new hardware products, you marry the software form factor with the hardware form factor. You can't think of them as completely separate, which is why it's difficult for companies to use off-the-shelf, commodity hardware and build truly excellent experiences.
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: One of the risks I see with some orgs that have both hardware and software is that they're so different that it's really hard to find a leader who can understand both worlds in depth. Similar to what you were saying about the general manager, sometimes it's hard to find someone who really gets both business and product right. So in your case, how do you actually find the right level of support to ensure that both hardware and software are at the same level of priority?
evidence.speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

evidence.quote: It's a good question. The biggest difference is the timelines are usually just different: building hardware takes longer than building software, and there are different steps you go through. To get really great outcomes, first you need incredible people. Two, you need to make sure the process you go through for building doesn't have a ton of burdensome red tape where decisions get mired in bureaucratic process or slow decision-making, because ultimately both building hardware and software is one of iteration. You have a vision of what you want to build, but the path there takes a bunch of different turns as you figure out what defect rates you're targeting, what reliability rates, battery life, and so on. There's a ton of dimensions to it. And then the best software is also built via an iterative learning loop. So if you combine both of those together, you can have both an org and a process that leads to incredible outcomes. The DRI Model: Killing the Silent Veto
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

entities.name: Buzz
entities.how_described: 本集说 Buzz 是 Block 新发布的产品，不是做某个单一渠道，而是帮卖家统一管理员工协作和所有渠道进来的客户消息

evidence.quote: Yeah, it's a great question. Business at its core is a communication, slash team, sport. You want to communicate with your customers, and you need to communicate with your staff. Today, a lot of that communication happens in very segmented, siloed tools, like you just mentioned: WhatsApp, Instagram, email. "I need a contractor to go fix something," and it's usually email, maybe text. When you talk to business owners, they are drowning in these many different communication tools. They'll say, "My SMS inbox has hundreds of unread." It's crazy. Just your example: imagine that business's WhatsApp thread, it's probably crazy. So, one, no one's really solved this yet, to be honest. Two, I'm pretty interested in trying to solve it for small businesses. There are some very cool collaboration platforms we're building. One is Buzz, which I think is pretty unique and interesting: not that exact product, but how that model could help sellers manage both their staff and a lot of communication inbounds across all these different channels they get.
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

evidence.quote: Yeah, I'll just go back to the fact that every business and every person has a communication challenge. Not actually talking, but managing all of the different channels. I don't think we have a great solution yet. I'm pretty excited about the Buzz technology for a lot of good reasons. It's something we're excited to work on.
evidence.speaker: Willem Avé

entities.name: 智能体AI (agentic AI)
entities.how_described: 本集说智能体 AI 真正允许卖家同时与多个不同软件产品互动，因为很多软件可以非常好地被智能体工具使用

evidence.quote: That's right. The challenge with that is, it used to be very difficult to build software for each of those quadrants. AI software engineering has lowered that bar to a certain degree. The second point is that a lot of customers and sellers have software solutions today that they like. So for us to be successful, we need both great first-party tools, point of sale, staff management tools, and so on, but also a very open platform to allow all of our incredible partners to build alongside us and with us, so we can help reduce a bunch of tabs and copying data between this tool and that tool to answer a question. And then the third is that AI, at least an agentic AI, really allows sellers to interact with a bunch of different software products at the same time, because a lot of software is able to be used very well by agentic tools. You see that today with Claude and Codex. They can just use these tools exceedingly well. So it's helping solve a lot of these multi-software challenges that customers have.
